question: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 together. The bat costs $1 more than the ball. How much is the ball?
answer: Five cents: the bat is $1.05, and together they make $1.10. Ten cents springs to mind first, and more than half of the students tested at Harvard, MIT and Princeton gave it. Kahneman's point: a fast system hands up the answer that feels right, and a slow one checks it only if it wakes up.
move: When an answer arrives instantly, check it as if a stranger had said it.
trap: Ten cents: it fits at a glance, so nothing checks it.
simply: Your brain has a fast friend who shouts the first answer, and a slow friend who does sums. The fast one shouted 'ten cents' before the slow one even looked up.
why: The same fast answer runs your first take on a price, a headline or a person. Knowing it is a guess is what lets you check it when it matters.
source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011
reference: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011), ch. 3
